question_text: Explore Webster's presentation of the Cardinal in The Duchess of Malfi.

content_markdown:
Webster presents the Cardinal as a man who treats religious office as a costume he can remove at will. The play uses him to expose the gap between sacred role and personal conduct, and to show how, in a corrupted court, even the apparatus of the Church can become an instrument of cruelty. Across his five acts of stage time, Webster develops the Cardinal from outwardly composed churchman to abandoned, theologically confused victim of his own machinations, and the trajectory drives the play's argument that ecclesiastical authority without ecclesiastical content is a particularly dangerous form of corruption.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster establishes the Cardinal's character before he speaks, by giving Antonio a long diagnostic description in 1.1. Antonio observes that "where he is jealous of any man, he lays worse plots for them than ever was imposed on Hercules" and that "he should have been Pope; but instead of coming to it by the primitive decency of the church, he did bestow bribes so largely, and so impudently, as if he would have carried it away without heaven's knowledge." **[AO2]** The choric report is dramatically deliberate — Webster wants the audience prejudiced against the Cardinal before they hear him speak — and the imagery of "engendering of toads" beneath the Cardinal's facial composure converts his apparent dignity into something demonic. The accusation of simony (buying ecclesiastical office) is the play's most precise contemporary critique. **[AO3]** Many in Webster's Protestant audience would have recognised the indictment as belonging to a polemical tradition stretching back to Luther's 95 Theses of 1517, in which Counter-Reformation Catholic ecclesiastical promotion was widely understood as conducted through bribery. The Italianate setting permits Webster to attack church corruption that he could not safely have attacked in the Stuart episcopal establishment.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster develops this idea visually at the start of Act 3, where the stage direction reads "He lays down his cardinal's habit and puts on a soldier's." **[AO2]** The on-stage costume change is a piece of theological theatre: the cardinal's red robes, biretta and pectoral cross are publicly removed, and martial armour is publicly assumed, in front of the audience. The dramatic statement is unmistakable — religious office is removable at convenience, and the same body can serve church and state with no inner change. **[AO3]** For many in Webster's audience, the moment may have resonated with contemporary concerns about Stuart bishops who served as royal councillors and political agents, blurring the boundary between ecclesiastical and political authority. The visual moment shows that the Cardinal's "religion" was never internalised; it is a coat he can take off.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster also presents the Cardinal as sexually corrupt, through his liaison with Julia. In their bedroom scene in 2.4 he speaks of women in conventional misogynistic vocabulary — "a man might strive to make glass malleable, / Ere he should make them fixed" — while himself committing adultery with another man's wife. **[AO2]** The dramatic irony is acute: the cleric who articulates the discipline he is paid to teach is the very person violating it, and Webster's stagecraft positions him in domestic, sexually intimate space rather than in the chapel where his office belongs. **[AO3]** Counter-Reformation Catholic discipline of clerical celibacy was a frequent target of Protestant satire in the period, and many in Webster's audience would have recognised Julia's bedroom as the appropriate location for exposing clerical hypocrisy. Webster's Cardinal is corrupt not because he sins, but because his sin and his office cohabit without friction.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster's most refined emblem of the Cardinal's corruption is the poisoning of Julia in 5.2, where he makes her swear secrecy by kissing a sacred book and then tells her: "thou'rt poison'd with that book." **[AO2]** Every detail of this stage business inverts a Catholic devotional gesture — the book is sacred, the kiss is liturgical, the swearing is theological — and Webster converts the entire apparatus of Catholic sacramental culture into the operative instrument of murder. The *Ars Moriendi*, the late-medieval tradition of dying well with sacramental preparation, is grotesquely inverted: Julia dies in the very act of swearing a perverted oath. **[AO3]** The Overbury affair of 1613 — political poisoning at the Stuart court by court favourites — gave the scene immediate contemporary resonance, and many in Webster's audience would have heard the poisoned-book episode as covert critique of Stuart court murder culture as well as Counter-Reformation Italy. The kiss of devotional adoration becomes the kiss of liquidation, and the Cardinal's character is fully exposed.

**[AO1 + AO2]** Webster brings the Cardinal's trajectory to its conclusion in 5.5, where he is murdered while his courtiers, watching from a balcony, refuse to come down. They mock his cries for help — "Some falling-out amongst the cardinals … / He doth this very often" — and the dramatic irony is deliberately savage: the Cardinal had earlier instructed them to ignore any cries from his apartment, and they obey his instruction by leaving him to die. **[AO2]** Webster's stagecraft here exposes the corrupted court as a system in which the very sycophants whose service authenticates the Cardinal's office now ratify his death by refusing to interrupt their performance of it. His dying speculation — "I am puzzled in a question about hell" — is dramatically extraordinary: the cleric whose vocation is to teach the catechism of last things is, at the moment of his own approach to those things, theologically lost. The ecclesiastical functionary has lived without theological seriousness, and the apparatus of his office offers no consolation in extremis. His final request — "let me / Be laid by, and never thought of" — is the renunciation of the very memorial apparatus his office had been constructed to provide.

**[Conclusion linked to question]** Webster therefore presents the Cardinal as the play's most refined diagnosis of ecclesiastical corruption: a churchman whose simoniacal *fama*, sartorial flexibility, sexual hypocrisy, sacramental weaponisation and abandoned death together expose religion treated as costume. He is dangerous not because he disbelieves, but because his belief and his office have come apart, and his death without comfort is Webster's exact judgement on a religious career conducted without religious content.
